subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
questions.explain: Carbohydrates such as starch and sugars are the body's main and most readily available source of energy.

questions.q: Which food is being tested for, and what colour is a positive result, when iodine solution turns blue-black?
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: A positive Benedict's test for reducing sugar produces which final colour when heated?
questions.explain: Benedict's solution changes from blue to brick-red when a reducing sugar such as glucose is present and heated.

questions.q: Which mineral is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells?
questions.explain: Iron is required to make haemoglobin, and a deficiency causes anaemia.

questions.q: In which organ is bile produced?
questions.explain: Bile is produced by the liver and then stored in the gall bladder before being released into the small intestine.

questions.q: Which acid is found in the stomach?
questions.explain: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which kills bacteria and gives the low pH needed by stomach enzymes.

questions.q: Amylase breaks down starch into which substance?
questions.explain: Amylase (a carbohydrase) digests starch into the sugar maltose.

questions.q: Lipase breaks down lipids into which two products?
questions.explain: Lipase digests lipids (fats and oils) into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.q: A food sample is tested with Biuret solution and turns purple/lilac. What does this show?
questions.explain: The Biuret test turns from blue to purple/lilac when protein is present.

questions.q: Why is dietary fibre an important part of a balanced diet?
options: It helps move food through the gut and prevents constipation
It is the body's main energy store
It is used for growth and repair of tissues
It is needed to make strong bones and teeth
questions.explain: Fibre (roughage) provides bulk that keeps food moving through the intestines, preventing constipation.

questions.q: A lack of which vitamin in the diet leads to the deficiency disease rickets?
questions.explain: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for healthy bones, so a deficiency causes rickets.

questions.q: How are the villi of the small intestine adapted for their function?
options: They give a large surface area for absorption
They store bile until it is needed
They churn food to mix it with enzymes
questions.explain: Villi have thin walls and a large surface area with a good blood supply, which speeds up the absorption of digested food.

questions.q: What is the main function of bile in the digestion of fats?
options: It emulsifies fats to increase their surface area
It breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol
It absorbs fats into the blood
questions.explain: Bile emulsifies large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on.

questions.q: Bile is alkaline. Why is this important in the small intestine?
options: It neutralises stomach acid to provide the optimum pH for enzymes
It kills bacteria that enter with food
It breaks down proteins into amino acids
questions.explain: Alkaline bile neutralises the acid from the stomach, giving the slightly alkaline pH that intestinal enzymes work best in.

questions.q: Which statement best describes digestive enzymes?
options: They are biological catalysts that speed up the breakdown of food
They are used up during the reactions they control
They are a type of carbohydrate that stores energy
They raise the temperature of the gut to digest food
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions, such as digestion, without being used up.

questions.q: What happens to a digestive enzyme if it is heated to a very high temperature?
options: It is denatured and stops working
It works faster and faster indefinitely
It turns into a different nutrient
questions.explain: Very high temperatures change the shape of the enzyme's active site, denaturing it so it can no longer break down its substrate.

questions.q: A person has bleeding gums and cuts that are slow to heal. A lack of which nutrient is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, with symptoms including bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

questions.q: Someone eats a meal that is very high in fat. The secretion of which enzyme would you expect to increase most to digest it?
questions.explain: Lipase digests fats, so more lipase is needed to break down a high-fat meal.

questions.q: An enzyme is found to work fastest at pH 2. In which part of the digestive system is it most likely to act?
questions.explain: Only the stomach is strongly acidic (around pH 2) because of its hydrochloric acid, matching this enzyme's optimum.

questions.q: After eating a protein-rich meal, in which organ does the chemical digestion of the protein first begin?
questions.explain: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where protease enzymes work in the acidic conditions to break protein into amino acids.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Biology (2017) specification; Nutrition & Health
